subtype: Approach: fixing a blocked exit found in the drill [Revision]
passage: On Sunday the school's safety club came round the staff quarters with a stopwatch, and it was the turn of Eshaan's flat. Neelam Ma'am rang the bell and said, "Go!" Eshaan and his sister Ritika ran for the balcony door, which would not budge. They tried the passage and hit a tall cupboard. It took almost three minutes. Their mother looked at the cupboard, then at the door. That afternoon the family pulled the cupboard aside and Papa oiled the latch. They ran the drill again, twice more, and on the third go the stopwatch showed fifty seconds. Ritika cheered.

qa.q: What blocked the passage in the drill?
qa.a: A tall cupboard blocked the passage.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when the balcony door would not budge?
qa.a: Alarmed and surprised, since the first try took almost three minutes.

qa.q: What else could the family do to keep the exits clear, and why?
qa.a: They could walk the route every month to check that nothing new blocks it, because clutter builds up slowly.

qa.q: How does Neelam Ma'am see the first slow attempt?
qa.a: Neelam Ma'am sees it as useful, since it shows the hidden problems that a drill is meant to find.

grounding: Children find a stuck door and blocked passage in a drill, and the family clears them and repeats the drill.

subtype: Approach: fixing a blocked exit found in the drill [Revision]
passage: I live on the same floor as the Rao family, and on Saturday I saw them doing their fire drill. Madhuri, the older girl, timed it on her mother's phone. On the first run, her brother Gautam pushed at the balcony door, their second exit, and it wouldn't budge. It was stuck. Then Madhuri tried the corridor and stopped: a big steel cupboard had been moved there during painting and half blocked the way. "Two minutes," she called. The whole family stood looking at the cupboard. That afternoon they pushed it back into the bedroom, and their father oiled the balcony door. They did the drill again. I heard Madhuri shout, "Fifty-two seconds!" I think they were happy with that.

qa.a: A big steel cupboard moved there during painting.

qa.q: How did the family seem to feel when they stood looking at the cupboard?
qa.a: They seemed surprised and concerned, realising their escape route had a real problem.

qa.q: What else could the family check during the next drill?
qa.a: They could check that the main door key is always in one known place, so nothing slows them at the door.

qa.q: How does the drill look to the neighbour?
qa.a: The neighbour sees the family find problems and fix them the same day, and seems to think they did well.

grounding: It shows children finding a stuck balcony door and a blocking cupboard during practice, and the family clearing the way and repeating the drill.

subtype: Approach: fixing a blocked exit found in the drill [Revision]
passage:
Sunday: Mehak and her brother Anirban ran the family's first fire drill with a kitchen timer. Out of their rooms, down the corridor, onto the balcony as the second exit. The balcony door stuck halfway. And the corridor was blocked by an old trunk. Time: two minutes, ten seconds.
Tuesday: Their mother moved the trunk to the loft. Their father planed the swollen edge of the balcony door until it swung open. Mehak tested it five times.
Saturday: They ran the drill again, from both bedrooms. No trunk. No stuck door. Anirban stopped the timer. "Fifty-five seconds." Mehak wrote it on the chart on the fridge and underlined it.

qa.q: How long did the first drill take?
How did Mehak feel when she wrote fifty-five seconds on the chart?
qa.a: She felt pleased and proud, underlining the time to show how much better it was.

qa.q: What else could the family plan after fixing the route?
qa.a: They could repeat the drill at night or with the lights off, since a real fire may come when it is dark.

qa.q: How does the drill look to Anirban?
qa.a: Anirban, holding the timer, sees the time drop and is likely pleased that the fixes worked.

grounding: It shows children finding a stuck door and a blocked corridor during a drill, the family clearing the way and repeating the drill until it takes under a minute.
